[muwu] It's obvious from the economics alone that's it's overwhelmingly a consumerism targeting non-specific ailments and "problems with living."
Thankfully homeostasis (i.e. renal filtration, hepatic metabolism) takes care of most of these abberations of supplementation that behavioural psychology leads to, not too dissimilar to how many of our actions and choices are handled by our own robust physiology.
Sure there are rare exceptions - I've seen the young woman needing a liver transplant due to the especially unusual toxicity of St. John's wort in her case, or the permanent peripheral neuropathy induced by supra therapeutic levels of vitamin B6. But as devastating as that can be, it is exceedingly rare.
Most of the damage is financial. But that's not limited to the consumerism of supplements, plenty of people know how to leak cash…
I've gone much deeper into supplementation than most doctors, due to a personal interest in fitness / performance, and a personal interest in health span / longevity, and I consider there being some light evidence for some select supplementation.
Firstly, most of this is achieved with nutrition. Whole foods, variety, you are dosing with more than adequate amounts of a vast number of micronutrients; diets, even relatively "poor" ones, can take care of business as the body latches onto what's needed if it's anywhere near a deficient state and filtrates out that which is less necessary. Supplementation is mostly just gilding the lily for what the human body has been balancing for millenia.
Magnesium is likely to be less than ideal levels in many of us, due to the nature of our agricultural practices. The problem is you really can't accurate test it, blood tests don't truly represent a "reserve" level; you could potentially see a neohrologist and do some more involved urinary testing, but even that is difficult to interpret. There's an argument for optimising magnesium in the form of evidence that it can provide a marginal benefit for reducing hypertension risk, and reducing metabolic dysfunction risk, which are both very important risk factors for common chronic / ageing diseases, like cardiovascular complications (heart disease, stroke) and diabetes. Forms of magnesium matter, as many are poorly absorbed and have more of a gastrointestinal profile, others are better absorbed and have better bioavailability. Hopefully you should limit your need to take much of it in supplement form, as many fruits and seeds/nuts are abundant with magnesium and have far superior absorption.
Vitamin D may be of seasonal benefit in select individuals. That usually affects populations in colder climates during winter, who spend an overwhelming amount of daytime hours indoors. Vitamin D can be easily measured on a blood test, and you're aiming for at least >30 but preferably >50, especially if tested mid-to-late winter when it nadirs. You are just aiming to be replete with vitamin D (please don't go down the optimisation funnel getting sucked into mega doses as a cure for everything), as you need the adequate amount to regulation calcium absorption and distribution physiologically, and supratheratpeutic levels, similar to artifical calcium supplementation, does show evidence of harm due to increasing calcium soft tissue depositing, like renal calcinosis (kidney disease) and atherosclerosis prolongation (heart attacks, strokes, vascular diseases).
Creatine is a performance enhancer, with little to no risk (renal filtration takes care of overdosing very effectively). You need to be putting in the work in the first place, so it's more important you are hitting your minimum standards for resistance training and aerobic stimulation per week. But the creatine can give you a few more percentage points, and as the benefits of exercise are of the greatest input to how well we age and preserve function and stave off disease and disability, the marginal help is welcome (but again, 98-99% of the great benefit comes from doing the thing, exercise is the Pareto principal, it's the nearest thing to a panacea for our bodies and its enviable slide, that and sleep close second).
That's it. Really, all of the others and the endless claims and beliefs and internet fodder telling you how important this and that supplement is, the evidence is just not there (and it's hard enough to find enough of a marginal benefit from the ones above).
Folate's definitely important for women trying to conceive. Folate and other methylated B vitamins may have broader metabolic benefits across life cycles, but that evidence is so weak it's nearly 0, and B vitamins are so readily available is food, especially with fortification, that an expensive supplement is a bit silly.
Iron will be important to some menstruating women who are struggling with anaemia. But the best source are haem-based foods (animal products), as oral iron supplements are awfully absorbed and have a bit of a nasty side effect profile. If a menstruating woman needs iron beyond diet, intravenous is the effective route (but more impotently gynaecological medical management).
The cheat here is not to even think about supplements as the thing that's gonna make the difference for you, but to rather have fun with food. Explore foods you haven't before, or new ways to prepare them. It's so exciting to think of the phenomenal broad nutritional benefits of a single food ingredient provides for your body, and then that's multiplied by all of the ingredients in a meal. Meal preparation aside, just the single discretionary foods, like a piece of fruit, is like having a mega-potent bioavailable multivitamin of everything on those expensive pharmacy selves, all served to you in a simple form you can bite into and savour and digest. Perfect 👍
Source: doctor
[Naigrabzo] Good advice my good sir. You are a scholar for sure.
[Jolakot] as the body latches onto what's needed if it's anywhere near a deficient state and filtrates out that which is less necessary
This is absolutely true, but in the same way that someone can survive with the bare essentials on Centrelink payments.
Giving your body more than it needs, or cares to extract from diet, does have real benefits for a couple more supplements.
Biotin is probably the biggest one, I could literally see the before/after effect in my fingernail after taking it for a few weeks. Your body does not give a crap about strong fingernails or shiny hair and the biotin you get from diet is diverted to more essential tasks, so only by supplementation can you flood your body with enough of the stuff for nails/hair to be saturated in it.
Same with vitamin B12 (intrinsic factor production is a hard limit for normal dietary absorption), vitamin B5, vitamin C, creatine, Glucosamine & Chondroitin (unless you eat tons of cartilage), Folate, L-Arginine, CoQ10, Magnesium etc
You just can't fully saturate your body by diet alone, it extracts what it needs to survive not what it can maximally use.
